incidents.title: Read-heavy feed
incidents.brief: An app is serving a personalized feed with 95% reads and a single primary database becomes saturated.
incidents.constraint: Almost all traffic is read-only and writes are relatively small.
incidents.question: What is the most direct fix?

choices.label: Add two read replicas and route the SELECTs to them
choices.resultBody: Two replicas take the SELECT traffic, so primary CPU drops from 95% to 31%. Cost: replicas lag the primary slightly, so a user may briefly read data older than their own write.

choices.label: Add app servers so each one handles fewer requests
choices.resultBody: The extra app servers open even more concurrent SELECTs against the single primary; its CPU hits 99% and p95 climbs from 3.2 s to 4 s.

choices.label: Batch writes into fewer commits to free primary CPU
choices.resultTitle: Writes batched, reads still crush it
choices.resultBody: Batching writes trims a little commit overhead, but reads are 95% of the load, so the primary stays at 97% CPU and p95 barely moves.

hints: Reads dominate this load.
Writes can stay on one primary.
Send reads to replicas.

incidents.title: Hourly finance report slows checkout
incidents.brief: ShopNova's finance report runs a 25-minute REPEATABLE READ query on the checkout MySQL primary every hour. The InnoDB history list grows to 8 million entries and checkout p95 jumps from 60 ms to 900 ms.
incidents.constraint: Finance accepts data up to 5 minutes old; checkout writes must stay on the primary.
incidents.question: Where should the report run so checkout recovers?

choices.label: Move the report to a dedicated reporting replica

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: Isolates heavy reads; reports lag by seconds.

choices.resultTitle: Report's snapshot moves off the primary
choices.resultBody: The long snapshot now holds back purge on the reporting replica only. The primary's history list drains to a few thousand entries, its CPU falls to 48%, and checkout p95 returns to 65 ms. Cost: one more replica, and report data is a few seconds old.

choices.label: Add a covering index so the report runs faster
choices.resultBody: The report drops from 25 to 12 minutes, but its snapshot still pins undo on the primary and the history list still reaches 4 million. The new index also slows every checkout insert, so p95 only improves to 500 ms.

choices.label: Run the report at READ UNCOMMITTED isolation
choices.resultTitle: Report totals no longer add up
choices.resultBody: Without a consistent snapshot the history list stops growing, but the report now counts orders that later rolled back and finance totals are off by 0.3%. Its full scans still burn primary CPU, and checkout p95 stays at 400 ms.

hints: Checkout slowed down even though its own traffic didn't change.
A long-running snapshot stops InnoDB from purging old row versions for everyone on that server.
Finance can tolerate minutes of lag; checkout can't share a server with that snapshot.

incidents.title: Profile edits vanish on refresh
incidents.brief: Linkly sends 8,000 reads/s to 3 async Postgres replicas. Lag averages 300 ms but spikes to 4 s during batch jobs, so 6% of profile edits look lost on refresh.
incidents.constraint: The primary is at 45% CPU; sending all reads back to it would push it past 95%.
incidents.question: How does a user always see their own edit?

choices.label: Session carries last-write LSN; route to a caught-up replica
choices.resultBody: After a write, the app stores the commit LSN in the session. Reads go to a replica whose replay LSN has passed it, and fall back to the primary only when none has (about 2% of reads). Cost: a lag check per read, cached for 100 ms, and session plumbing in every service.

choices.label: Route the user's reads to the primary for 1 second after writing
choices.resultBody: Stale own-reads drop to about 150/min, but during batch jobs lag reaches 4 s, well past the 1-second pin, so edits still vanish exactly when load is highest.

choices.label: Add a fourth replica to spread read load and cut lag
choices.resultBody: A fourth replica lowers read CPU from 58% to 44%, but lag comes from replaying batch writes, not from read load; stale own-reads stay around 460/min.

hints: Only the person who just wrote is affected.
A fixed time window fails whenever lag is longer than the window.
The primary can tell you exactly which position in its log contains the user's write.

incidents.title: Evening price lookups outgrow two replicas
incidents.brief: PriceWatch peaks at 70,000 reads/s every evening on 2 Postgres replicas that each top out near 18,000 reads/s. Both hit 99% CPU while the primary handles 1,500 writes/s at 35%.
incidents.constraint: Prices may be 2 s stale, and replicas must stay under 70% CPU at peak.
incidents.question: How many replicas does the evening peak need?

choices.label: Grow to six replicas at about 12k reads/s each

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: Sized for peak with headroom; costs more off-peak.

choices.resultBody: 70,000 reads/s over 6 replicas is about 11,700 each, roughly 65% of an 18,000 reads/s ceiling, so the peak fits under the 70% target and p95 falls to 25 ms. Cost: four more replicas, about $2,400 a month, and more WAL streams from the primary.

choices.label: Add one replica, making three for the peak
choices.resultBody: Three replicas split 70,000 reads/s into about 23,300 each, above the 18,000 ceiling, so all three sit at 99% CPU. Timeouts fall only slightly, to 5%.

choices.label: Send peak overflow reads to the primary
choices.resultBody: The primary picks up about 34,000 reads/s on top of its writes and CPU jumps from 35% to 97%. Price updates now queue behind reads, write latency passes 2 s, and replicas start lagging too.

hints: Work out reads per replica at peak, not on average.
Each replica has a ceiling, and the target is 70% of it.
Divide the peak by 70% of one replica's capacity and round up.

incidents.title: Replicas fall 20 minutes behind by noon
incidents.brief: LedgerLite's MySQL primary commits 9,000 small transactions/s across 16 cores. Its 3 replicas apply the binlog on a single SQL thread, top out near 5,000 transactions/s, and trail 20 minutes by noon.
incidents.constraint: Balance pages read from replicas and must be less than 5 s stale.
incidents.question: What lets the replicas keep up with the primary?

choices.label: Parallel binlog apply with LOGICAL_CLOCK workers

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: Apply throughput matches the primary; more replica CPU.

choices.resultTitle: Replicas apply as fast as the primary commits
choices.resultBody: With WRITESET dependency tracking on the primary and 16 apply workers that preserve commit order, each replica applies about 14,000 transactions/s. The 20-minute backlog drains in about 25 minutes and lag then stays under 1 s. Cost: replica CPU rises to about 45%.

choices.label: Add three more replicas to spread balance reads
choices.resultBody: Every new replica replays the same 9,000 transactions/s on one thread and falls behind at the same rate. Reads are spread wider, but every balance page is still minutes stale.

choices.label: Upgrade every replica to a 64-core instance
choices.resultBody: The apply thread still uses one core, and the other 63 idle, so throughput stays near 5,000 transactions/s. Lag keeps growing and the replica bill quadruples.

hints: Replica CPU looks low, but one core on each is at 100%.
The primary commits in parallel on 16 cores, and each replica replays it serially.
Transactions that don't touch the same rows can be applied at the same time.

incidents.title: Meter ingest pegs the primary at 95%
incidents.brief: GridSense writes 60,000 meter readings/s into one Postgres primary as single-row INSERTs, each its own transaction and fsync. Dashboards read only 300 queries/s. The primary sits at 95% CPU.
incidents.constraint: Readings must be durable within 1 s of arrival; the team can make one change this sprint.
incidents.question: What actually takes load off the primary?

choices.label: Batch readings into one COPY per second per worker

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: Far fewer commits for up to 1 s of added write latency.

choices.resultBody: Twenty ingest workers buffer for up to 1 s and COPY about 3,000 rows each per transaction. Commits and fsyncs fall from 60,000/s to 20/s and primary CPU drops to 40%. Cost: workers acknowledge only after commit, so meters resend up to 1 s of readings on a crash.

choices.label: Add three read replicas behind the reader endpoint
choices.resultBody: The replicas take the 300 dashboard queries/s, which were never the problem. The primary still performs 60,000 commits/s at 95% CPU, and each replica now replays all 60,000 rows/s on top.

choices.label: Promote a replica to accept half of the meter inserts
choices.resultBody: Promoting a replica breaks it off from the original primary. Each node now holds half the readings, dashboards see incomplete data, and the two timelines can't be merged back without a manual rebuild.

hints: Look at the ratio of writes to reads.
Every replica must apply every write the primary makes.
Most of the primary's work is per transaction, not per row.

incidents.title: Pages slow while three replicas sit idle
incidents.brief: RecipeBox added 3 read replicas, but its framework opens a transaction for every request and the read/write router sends anything inside a transaction to the primary. The primary serves 30,000 reads/s at 93%.
incidents.constraint: Pages may show data up to 2 s old, but save flows must read their own writes.
incidents.question: How do the replicas start taking page reads?

choices.label: Mark GET handlers read-only so they route to replicas

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: Uses existing replicas; needs routing discipline in code.

choices.resultTitle: Page reads move to the replicas
choices.resultBody: GET handlers now open read-only transactions, which the router sends to replicas; saves and their follow-up reads stay on the primary. The primary drops to 35% CPU, replicas run near 55%, and p95 falls to 90 ms. Cost: a handler audit, and GETs that write, like view counters, must move.

choices.label: Point the whole app's connection string at one replica
choices.resultBody: Page reads move off the primary, but replicas reject writes with "cannot execute INSERT in a read-only transaction". Every recipe save, rating, and login update fails, which is 12% of all requests.

choices.label: Add two more replicas to the router's reader pool
choices.resultTitle: Five idle replicas instead of three
choices.resultBody: The router still sees every query inside a transaction and sends it to the primary. The two new replicas join the others at 4% CPU while the primary stays at 93%.

hints: The replicas are healthy and caught up, but receive no queries.
The router decides by the kind of transaction, not by the SQL inside it.
Tell the router which requests only read.

incidents.title: Archive export wipes the replicas' cache
incidents.brief: Newsly's 4 replicas serve 40,000 article reads/s from a warm cache. A daily compliance export now scans 5 years of archives on the same pool; cache hit rate falls from 98% to 55% and p95 from 30 ms to 700 ms.
incidents.constraint: The export runs daily this quarter; the 4 replicas are all the budget allows.
incidents.question: How do you keep the export from hurting readers?

choices.label: Tag export queries and route them to replica 4

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: Contains cache damage to one node at the cost of pool headroom.

choices.resultBody: The proxy sends queries tagged as the export to replica 4 only and takes it out of the reader pool. Replicas 1-3 keep a 98% hit rate and carry the 40,000 reads/s at about 72% CPU, and p95 returns to 35 ms. Cost: less reader headroom while the export runs.

choices.label: Double the replicas' RAM so the archive fits in cache
choices.resultBody: The archive is 6 TB and the replicas now have 512 GB each, so the scan still pushes hot articles out of cache on all 4 nodes. The hit rate only recovers to 62% and the RAM bill doubles.

choices.label: Run the export on the primary overnight instead
choices.resultTitle: Primary's cache takes the hit instead
choices.resultBody: Readers recover, but the scan now evicts the primary's working set. Morning publishing writes hit a cold cache, commit latency passes 400 ms, and the scan load makes all 4 replicas lag by 90 s.

hints: Replica CPU is moderate; the damage shows up in the cache hit rate.
A full archive scan pushes the hot articles out of every cache it passes through.
Decide which replicas the scan is allowed to touch.

incidents.title: One replica serves 40-second-old feeds
incidents.brief: PicShare round-robins 60,000 feed reads/s across 4 MySQL replicas. Replica 3's disk is degraded and it lags 40 s, so a quarter of feeds miss recent posts.
incidents.constraint: The other three replicas lag under 200 ms and each has about 35% CPU headroom.
incidents.question: How do you keep the lagging replica from serving users?

choices.label: Health-check replica lag and eject any above 1 s
choices.resultBody: ProxySQL polls each replica's replication delay every second and stops routing to replica 3 at 40 s; the other three absorb its 15,000 reads/s and rise to about 80% CPU. Cost: a quarter less read headroom until the disk is replaced, so ejections need an alert and a minimum-pool floor.

choices.label: Switch the balancer from round-robin to least-connections
choices.resultBody: Least-connections weighs open connections, not how current a replica is; replica 3 still answers quickly from memory, keeps its share, and 24% of feeds stay 40 s stale.

choices.label: Route every feed read to the primary until lag clears
choices.resultBody: Feeds are fresh, but 60,000 reads/s land on a primary sized for writes; its CPU jumps from 50% to 97% and feed p95 climbs from 90 ms to 1.4 s.

hints: Only one of the four replicas is behind.
Round-robin knows whether a replica is up, not whether it is current.
Routing can use a freshness signal each replica already reports.

incidents.title: One replica at 95% while two sit idle
incidents.brief: MapTiles' app servers open long-lived connection pools to the reader DNS name at boot. After a replica restart, 80% of connections ended up on replica 1: it runs at 95% CPU while replicas 2 and 3 sit near 20%.
incidents.constraint: App servers restart only once a week.
incidents.question: How do reads spread evenly across the replicas again?

choices.label: Route reads through a proxy that balances per query

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: Even replica load regardless of client pooling; another tier to run.

choices.resultBody: Apps connect to a ProxySQL pair, which keeps its own pools to every replica and spreads each query by load. All three replicas settle near 45% CPU and p95 drops to 40 ms. Cost: about 0.3 ms per query and a proxy tier to keep highly available.

choices.label: Add a fourth replica to the reader DNS round-robin
choices.resultBody: Existing pools never re-resolve the DNS name, so the new replica receives nothing until next week's restarts. Replica 1 stays at 95% and the new node idles at 2%.

choices.label: Cap replica 1 at 200 connections in its config
choices.resultBody: Replica 1 starts refusing new connections with "too many connections", and pools that lose a connection fail to replace it. 15% of tile reads error until pools happen to resolve another replica.

hints: All three replicas are healthy and caught up.
DNS picks a replica once per connection, and these connections live for a week.
Balancing needs to happen per query, by something that sees every replica.

incidents.title: Typeahead queries swamp Postgres
incidents.brief: BookNook's search box fires 12,000 suggestion queries/s using ILIKE '%term%' on a 20M-row titles table. Each one is a 300 ms sequential scan, and the primary and both replicas sit at 99% CPU.
incidents.constraint: Budget allows at most two more database instances.
incidents.question: What makes each suggestion cheap enough to serve?

choices.label: Build a pg_trgm GIN index for the ILIKE lookups

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: Cuts per-query cost 100x; extra index storage and write cost.

choices.resultBody: A pg_trgm GIN index built CONCURRENTLY on the primary replicates to both replicas, and ILIKE on terms of 3+ characters now uses it. Each suggestion costs about 3 ms, so replicas fall to 30% CPU. Cost: a 1.5 GB index and slightly slower title writes.

choices.label: Add two more replicas just for suggestion traffic
choices.resultTitle: Two replicas against 3,600 cores of work
choices.resultBody: 12,000 queries/s at 300 ms of CPU each needs about 3,600 cores. Two more 32-core replicas add 64, so all four replicas sit at 99% and timeouts barely move.

choices.label: Create a plain B-tree index on the title column
choices.resultBody: A B-tree only helps prefix matches like 'term%'. With a leading wildcard the planner still chooses a sequential scan, so CPU stays at 99% and the new index just adds write cost.

hints: Replicas multiply capacity; they don't make a query cheaper.
Multiply queries per second by CPU time per query.
A leading wildcard needs an index built from pieces of each word.

incidents.title: BI dashboards crush the dispatch database
incidents.brief: FleetOps analysts run 40 BI dashboards straight against the OLTP Postgres primary, each scanning 200M-row trip tables. At 9 a.m. the primary hits 90% CPU and dispatch writes slow to 800 ms.
incidents.constraint: BI data may be 15 minutes old, and analysts must be able to create their own tables.
incidents.question: Where should the analytics workload live?

choices.label: Stream changes via CDC into a columnar warehouse

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: Right engine for scans; a pipeline to operate.

choices.resultBody: Debezium reads the primary's WAL through a logical replication slot and lands changes in a columnar warehouse about 2 minutes later. Dashboards scan compressed columns in seconds, analysts own their schema, and primary CPU falls to 45%. Cost: monitor the slot, because an unconsumed slot keeps WAL and fills the disk.

choices.label: Give the analysts a physical read replica
choices.resultBody: Dispatch recovers, but a physical standby is read-only, so CREATE TABLE fails. Long dashboard queries are also cancelled with "conflict with recovery" whenever vacuum on the primary removes rows they still need, and 35% of BI queries fail.

choices.label: Nightly pg_dump restored into an analytics copy
choices.resultBody: The dump takes 3 hours of primary I/O each night, and dashboards show data up to 24 hours old, far past the 15-minute limit. Morning fleet planning runs on stale trips.

hints: The analysts need to write their own tables, not just read.
A physical replica is a byte-for-byte, read-only copy of the primary.
Row stores and column stores are good at different queries; changes can flow from one to the other.

incidents.title: Bookings fail with "read-only transaction"
incidents.brief: After a planned failover, CarePlus's old primary rejoined as a replica. App pools opened before the switch still point at it, so 30% of appointment bookings fail with "cannot execute INSERT in a read-only transaction".
incidents.constraint: Failovers happen monthly for patching; nobody wants a manual app restart each time.
incidents.question: How should the app find the current writer on its own?

choices.label: Connect with target_session_attrs=read-write

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: Self-healing writer discovery; brief errors at each failover.

choices.resultBody: The connection string lists both hosts, and libpq keeps only the one accepting writes. The pool also discards any connection that returns a read-only error, so bookings recover within seconds of each failover. Cost: a few seconds of errors during every switch.

choices.label: Retry failed bookings three times on the same pool
choices.resultBody: Each retry borrows another stale connection to the old primary and gets the same read-only error. Failed bookings stay near 29%, and the retries triple the load on the replica.

choices.label: Promote the old primary back so it accepts writes
choices.resultBody: Both nodes now accept writes and neither replicates to the other. Within minutes the same 9:00 slot is booked twice on different nodes, and the two histories can't be merged cleanly.

hints: The database is healthy; the app is talking to the wrong node.
Connections opened before the failover still go to the old primary's address.
The client can check whether a server accepts writes before it keeps a connection.

incidents.title: Two million phones poll the primary
incidents.brief: PingMe's 2 million active devices poll GET /unread every 30 s, about 66,000 queries/s, all on the Postgres primary. It sits at 96% CPU and new-message writes now take 1.2 s.
incidents.constraint: New messages must reach devices within 30 s; the unread count may lag by a few seconds.
incidents.question: Where should the poll queries go?

choices.label: Serve the unread-count poll from a replica pool

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: Offloads tolerant reads; counts lag by milliseconds.

choices.resultBody: The poll endpoint reads from 4 replicas that lag about 200 ms, about 16,500 queries/s each at 60% CPU. The primary keeps only writes and drops to 30%, and new-message writes return to 15 ms. Cost: four replicas, and counts may trail a new message by a fraction of a second.

choices.label: Stretch the poll interval from 30 s to five minutes
choices.resultBody: Queries drop tenfold and the primary recovers, but a new message now takes up to 5 minutes to appear. That breaks the 30-second promise for nearly every message sent.

choices.label: Cache each user's poll response in app memory
choices.resultBody: Polls are spread round-robin over 40 app servers, so each server sees a given device about once every 20 minutes. Entries expire before reuse, the hit rate is about 3%, and the primary stays at 94%.

hints: Almost all of the primary's load is the same read, repeated.
The product allows the unread count to be a few seconds behind.
Reads that tolerate a little lag don't need the node that takes writes.

incidents.title: Standby idles while the primary hits 92%
incidents.brief: TaxEase's RDS primary runs at 92% CPU during filing season. Its Multi-AZ standby sits in another zone at 5% CPU, and the team wants to use it for 18,000 reads/s of return-status lookups.
incidents.constraint: The database is on the largest instance class already, and zone-failure protection must stay.
incidents.question: How do you add read capacity without weakening failover?

choices.label: Add read replicas; keep the standby for failover

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: Separates read scale from HA; pay for both.

choices.resultBody: Two async read replicas take the 18,000 lookups/s at about 55% CPU with around 100 ms of lag. The synchronous standby keeps its only job, so a zone failure still fails over with no lost commits, and primary CPU drops to 40%. Cost: two more instances.

choices.label: Convert the standby into a lookup read replica
choices.resultBody: Lookups move and the primary recovers, but there is no synchronous standby any more. If the primary's zone fails, promoting the async replica takes minutes and can lose the last few seconds of submitted returns.

choices.label: Shard tax returns across two primaries by state
choices.resultTitle: Months of work for a read problem
choices.resultBody: Splitting the schema, rewriting cross-state queries, and migrating data takes a quarter. Filing season ends first, and the primary stays at 92% CPU for the rest of it.

hints: The standby exists for one reason, and it isn't serving reads.
High availability and read scaling are separate jobs.
Asynchronous copies can take reads while the synchronous one waits for a failure.

incidents.title: Flash sale oversells items already gone
incidents.brief: GearHub serves 50,000 product-page reads/s from replicas that lag 1-3 s on sale days. Stock counts come from the same replicas, so 6% of add-to-cart clicks in a flash sale reserve items that already sold out.
incidents.constraint: The primary can absorb about 3,000 extra queries/s; add-to-cart runs at 2,000/s.
incidents.question: Which reads must go to the primary?

choices.label: Reserve stock on the primary at add-to-cart

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: Strong reads only where money is at stake.

choices.resultTitle: Only the decision point reads fresh data
choices.resultBody: Browsing stays on replicas, but add-to-cart runs UPDATE stock = stock - 1 WHERE stock > 0 on the primary, which reserves and checks in one atomic step. 2,000 extra queries/s lift the primary to 62% and oversells drop to 0. Cost: add-to-cart pays a primary round trip.

choices.label: Route all product reads to the primary on sale days
choices.resultBody: Stock is always fresh, but 50,000 reads/s land on a primary sized for writes plus a small margin. CPU hits 99%, stock updates queue behind page views, and p95 climbs to 2.4 s mid-sale.

choices.label: Switch the replicas to synchronous replication
choices.resultBody: With synchronous_commit on, commits wait for replicas to flush WAL, not to apply it, so a replica can still return a stock count from before the last sale. Oversells only fall to 4%, and every write gains about 3 ms.

hints: Most reads here can be seconds old; a few can't.
The harm happens at one step: deciding whether an item is still available.
Make the check and the reservation a single step on the node that owns the truth.

incidents.title: Sydney pages take 1.2 s on an idle database
incidents.brief: TravelNest runs app servers in Sydney but its Postgres primary in us-east-1. Each page makes 6 sequential SELECTs at ~190 ms RTT, so pages take 1.2 s while the primary idles at 40% CPU.
incidents.constraint: Bookings must commit on the US primary, browse data may be seconds stale, and the target p95 is under 300 ms.
incidents.question: What brings read latency down for Sydney users?

choices.label: Cross-region read replica in Sydney for browse queries
choices.resultBody: Browse SELECTs now hit a replica about 1 ms away, so six queries cost ~15 ms instead of 1.1 s and pages load in about 180 ms. Cost: replication lag of a few hundred ms (more under write bursts), cross-region transfer fees, and bookings still pay a 190 ms round-trip to the US.

choices.label: Upgrade the US primary to twice the vCPUs
choices.resultBody: Each query now executes in 1 ms instead of 2 ms, but the 190 ms round-trip dominates; six sequential trips still cost about 1.14 s and bounce rate stays near 37%.

choices.label: Move the Sydney app servers to us-east-1 beside the database
choices.resultTitle: One ocean crossing instead of six
choices.resultBody: Queries are now local, but every Sydney request and its TLS handshake crosses the Pacific; pages settle around 450 ms, better than 1.2 s but still over the 300 ms target.

hints: The database is not busy; the time goes somewhere else.
Count the round-trips per page and multiply by the RTT.
Reads that tolerate staleness can come from a copy near the users.

incidents.title: Reporting replica is 3 hours behind
incidents.brief: FinLedger's replica falls 3 hours behind every afternoon. A BI dashboard opens a transaction and leaves it idle, and with max_standby_streaming_delay = -1 WAL replay waits for it.
incidents.constraint: The same replica serves customer statement pages, which must be less than 1 minute stale.
incidents.question: How do you keep replay moving on this replica?

choices.label: Kill idle transactions after 5 min; cap replay wait at 30 s
choices.resultBody: idle_in_transaction_session_timeout ends the abandoned dashboard session, and max_standby_streaming_delay = 30s lets replay cancel any query blocking it longer than that. Lag falls from 3 hours to under 30 s. Cost: long analyst queries that conflict with replay get canceled and must retry, or move to a separate reporting copy.

choices.label: Turn on hot_standby_feedback so vacuum spares old rows
choices.resultTitle: Lag gone, bloat on the primary
choices.resultBody: Replay no longer hits vacuum conflicts, but the 3-hour-old snapshot now stops autovacuum on the primary; dead rows pile up, the ledger table bloats by 40 GB, and primary CPU climbs from 38% to 58%.

choices.label: Add a second reporting replica to share dashboard load
choices.resultBody: The dashboard's idle transaction simply opens on the new replica too; by 15:00 both replicas are hours behind and statement pages are still about 3 hours stale.

hints: Lag isn't caused by load; the replica is waiting on something.
Look for a session that has been 'idle in transaction' for hours.
Replay needs a limit on how long any single query may hold it back.

incidents.title: Session lookups keep the primary at 94%
incidents.brief: StudyHub stores sessions in a Postgres table on the primary. Every request reads its session and updates last_seen, so 45,000 req/s become 45,000 writes/s, and the primary sits at 94% CPU.
incidents.constraint: Sessions expire after 30 idle minutes; losing one only forces a re-login.
incidents.question: Where should sessions live?

choices.label: Move sessions to Redis with a 30-minute sliding TTL

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: Ephemeral data in an ephemeral store; logouts if Redis is lost.

choices.resultBody: Each request now does a Redis GET and EXPIRE, about 0.3 ms, and Redis drops idle sessions itself. The primary sheds 45,000 writes/s and falls to 40% CPU, and p95 returns to 60 ms. Cost: a Redis pair to run, and a Redis loss logs everyone out.

choices.label: Read sessions from the replica, keep updates on the primary
choices.resultBody: The last_seen updates are still 45,000 writes/s on the primary. New sessions also haven't replicated when the next request arrives, so 8% of logins bounce straight back to the login page.

choices.label: Add an index on the session token column
choices.resultTitle: Index adds cost to every hit
choices.resultBody: Lookups already use the primary key, so reads gain nothing. Every last_seen update now maintains one more index, and primary CPU rises to 96%.

hints: Count the writes, not just the reads.
Replicas can take reads, but every write still lands on the primary.
This data expires on its own and is cheap to lose.

incidents.title: Schema change leaves replicas 40 minutes behind
incidents.brief: A plain ALTER TABLE adding a column to KartKing's 400M-row orders table ran 40 minutes on the MySQL primary, then replayed for 40 more on each replica. Product pages served 40-minute-old data.
incidents.constraint: Three more column changes to this table ship this month.
incidents.question: How do you run the next change without the replica lag?

choices.label: Online migration with gh-ost throttled on lag

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: Slow, throttled migration; replicas stay fresh.

choices.resultTitle: Schema changed, replicas never fell behind
choices.resultBody: gh-ost copies rows into a shadow table in small chunks, tails the binlog for new writes, and pauses whenever replica lag passes 1 s. The copy takes 6 hours, but lag stays under 1 s and the cut-over is an atomic rename. Cost: double the table's disk space during the copy.

choices.label: Run the ALTER at 3 a.m. when traffic is at its lowest
choices.resultBody: The replicas still replay the ALTER as one statement and fall 40 minutes behind. Night-shift shoppers see stale prices and stock, and the next three changes each need a 3 a.m. window.

choices.label: Send all reads to the primary during the ALTER
choices.resultBody: Pages are fresh, but 30,000 reads/s join the ALTER's I/O on the primary. CPU hits 99%, checkout writes wait behind page reads, and p95 climbs past 2 s for the whole 80 minutes.

hints: The primary ran the ALTER online; the replicas are the ones that fell behind.
A replica applies one huge DDL statement as a single, blocking unit of work.
Break the change into small copies that can pause when the replicas fall behind.

incidents.title: Primary host lost; every order write fails
incidents.brief: OrderFlow's Postgres primary lost its host at 14:02 and 2,400 writes/s are failing. Replica A lags 80 ms, replica B lags 9 s, and the old primary may reboot any minute.
incidents.constraint: Lose at most a second of committed orders, and the old primary must never accept writes again.
incidents.question: How do you restore writes safely?

choices.label: Promote the 80 ms replica and fence the old primary
choices.resultBody: Replica A is promoted in about 20 s, replica B is repointed to follow it, and the old primary is fenced (power cut via STONITH) so it cannot rejoin as a writer. Cost: up to 80 ms of unreplicated commits, about 190 orders, must be reconciled from the payment log, and read capacity drops by one node until the host is rebuilt.

choices.label: Promote whichever replica answers the health check first
choices.resultBody: Replica B answered first but was 9 s behind; promoting it discarded about 21,600 committed orders, and replica A now holds rows the new primary never saw, so it cannot follow it without a rebuild.

choices.label: Reboot the old primary's host and wait for it to return
choices.resultBody: The host takes 11 minutes to boot and run crash recovery; about 1.6 million write attempts fail in the meantime, and the disk that failed may fail again tonight.

hints: Two replicas can be promoted, but they are not equally current.
Promotion is only half the job: the old node could come back believing it is still primary.
Choose by replication position, then make sure only one writer can ever exist.

incidents.title: Reporting replica drifts 25 minutes behind
incidents.brief: PayPort's only reporting replica is a burstable db.t3.medium. Its CPU credit balance hit 0, CPU sits flat at its 20% baseline, and replay lag has grown to 25 minutes.
incidents.constraint: Report load is a steady 800 queries/s, and statements must be under 1 minute stale.
incidents.question: What gets the replica back under a minute of lag?

choices.label: Upsize the replica to a fixed-performance m6i.large

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: About $70 a month more for a replica that no longer runs out of CPU credits.

choices.resultBody: The m6i.large gives the replica its full two vCPUs all the time instead of a 20% baseline. Replay and reports together use about 45%, lag drains to 2 s within the hour, and report p95 falls to 180 ms. Cost: about $70 a month.

choices.label: Add two more burstable replicas behind a reader endpoint
choices.resultBody: Reads spread three ways, but every replica replays every write, and replay alone needs more than the 20% baseline. The new replicas burn through their launch credits by the next day and all three drift behind together.

choices.label: Replace it with a logical replica that skips cold tables
choices.resultTitle: Weeks of work on the same starved box
choices.resultBody: Setting up publications and an initial sync of the hot tables takes weeks. Logical apply still runs on a t3.medium with no credits, so even the smaller stream falls behind whenever reports run.

hints: A flat CPU line at exactly 20% is suspicious on a burstable instance.
Every replica, however many you add, replays the full write stream.
The replica is not short of design; it is short of guaranteed CPU.
